content:
I'm an independent researcher. Full provenance up front: both the Lean in this project and this post itself were AI-drafted (Claude, working in Cursor) under my direction and review which is why I'm posting in this channel. I committed in an earlier thread (April, #new members) to human-written posts after moderators flagged AI-drafted prose; I'm treating this channel as the one place where AI-drafted-and-disclosed is coherent with the venue's purpose rather than against it. If the moderators see that differently, tell me and I'll adjust.

On the mathematics: every principal claim is kernel-checked — no sorry, no native_decide, and per-theorem #print axioms audits reporting at most propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound.

The project formalizes some structure theory of one-generated Heyting algebras, against Mathlib4:

  • Nishimura's one-variable normal-form theorem: every element of the subalgebra generated by an element g is the value of a Rieger–Nishimura term in g. I couldn't find this in Mathlib or elsewhere in Lean.
  • Uniqueness of the ordinary element: call an element ordinary (Citkin's term) if it is neither regular (¬¬a = a) nor dense (¬a = ⊥). In any Heyting algebra one-generated by an ordinary element, the generator is the unique ordinary element. The statement appears without proof in Citkin's arXiv:2512.05633; he confirmed by correspondence (cited with permission) that he knew of no written proof, so the formalization is, as far as either of us knows, the first proof written down.
  • Supporting results: all four "regions" (below a / below ¬a / below ¬¬a but not a / meeting both a and ¬a) are inhabited iff a is ordinary; any algebra with an ordinary element has ≥ 6 elements and order-embeds the six-element one-generated algebra Z₆; an 8-element counterexample showing unique-ordinary does not imply one-generated; the divisor lattice of 12 is one-generated (≅ Z₆); an exact count formula for ordinary elements of products of chains; and End(Z₆) ≅ Z₆ with every endomorphism satisfying f³ = f — a small kernel-checked instance of Ruitenburg's 1984 periodicity theorem.

Source: https://github.com/thefalsework/papers — Lean in lean/FalseWorkPapers/Examples/, paper (with the theorem-by-Lean-name audit table in §10) in preprints/ordinary-elements-z6/.

Two questions for the room:

  1. Has anyone formalized (or started) Ruitenburg's theorem — for every A(p) in IPC the iteration sequence Aⁿ(p) is eventually periodic with period 2? The one-variable infrastructure here (Nishimura terms, the ladder, generated subalgebras) seems like most of the prerequisites, and I'd be glad to see it used for that.
  2. Would any of this be welcome in Mathlib (e.g. the ordinary/regular/dense trichotomy for Heyting algebras, or the Rieger–Nishimura ladder)? Happy to carve out PRs if so.

Corrections very welcome.

Follow-up: in another thread in this channel, the advice given to AI-authored projects was to provide a Challenge.lean importing only Mathlib, a Solution.lean importing the project code, comparator verification, and a formalization.yaml. This project now has all four, and CI is green:

  • lean/Challenge.lean — imports Mathlib only; states the six principal theorems with sorry, definitions inlined, ~120 lines: https://github.com/thefalsework/papers/blob/main/lean/Challenge.lean
  • lean/Solution.lean — imports the project code that proves them: https://github.com/thefalsework/papers/blob/main/lean/Solution.lean
  • comparator runs in CI on every push (config at lean/config.json; permitted axioms propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound): https://github.com/thefalsework/papers/actions/workflows/comparator.yml
  • formalization.yaml at the repo root, with the AI-usage disclosure (all Lean was AI-authored under my direction; I'm not a Lean reader), the theorem-by-theorem audit table, scope files, and known gaps stated: https://github.com/thefalsework/papers/blob/main/formalization.yaml

Comparator certifies proof-matches-statement; the link I can't close myself is statement-matches-paper. Three deliberate deviations from the paper's prose are documented in formalization.yaml: ordinary_forces_card_ge_six adds [Fintype H] (the infinite case is carried by the embedding theorem); ordinary_gives_z6_embedding asserts existence of the order-embedding rather than exhibiting the paper's explicit map; twelve_unique_kernel is stated on Fin 3 × Fin 2 rather than the literal divisor lattice (the kernel-checked iso div12OrderIsoChains bridges them inside the library). If anyone is willing to read Challenge.lean against the paper's claims, that is exactly the review I'm asking for.

(As disclosed above: the Lean and the prose of this post are AI-drafted; direction and review are mine.)
